concept_definition: A chemical element (symbol O) essential for respiration, making up about 21% of Earth's atmosphere.
A colorless gas (CO₂) produced by burning carbon and organic compounds and by respiration, absorbed by plants in photosynthesis.
A soft, silvery-white chemical element (symbol Li), the lightest metal, used in batteries and psychiatric medication.
The lightest and most abundant chemical element (symbol H), a colorless, odorless gas that combines with oxygen to form water.
A chemical element (symbol N) that is a colorless, odorless gas making up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere, essential for plant growth.
A pungent, colorless gas (NH₃) composed of nitrogen and hydrogen, widely used in fertilizers, cleaning products, and industrial chemistry.
A colorless, odorless, flammable gas (CH₄) that is the main component of natural gas and a significant greenhouse gas.
A chemical element (symbol Cl) that is a yellow-green, toxic gas with a pungent smell, commonly used to disinfect water and in manufacturing.
a chemical substance with a pH below 7 that can dissolve metals and turn litmus paper red.
a chemical substance with a pH above 7 that can neutralize acids and turn litmus paper blue.
The smallest unit of a chemical compound that retains the compound’s chemical properties, consisting of two or more atoms bonded together.
An atom or molecule that has gained or lost one or more electrons and therefore carries an electric charge.
A soft, highly reactive chemical element with the symbol Na and atomic number 11, commonly found in compounds such as salt.
A salt or ester of carbonic acid, containing the carbonate ion CO₃²⁻.
A chemical compound containing chlorine combined with another element or group, especially a salt in which chlorine exists as the negatively charged ion Cl⁻.
A stable subatomic particle with a negative electric charge, found outside the nucleus of an atom and involved in electricity, chemical bonding, and radiation.
A chemical element with atomic number 6, occurring in all known living organisms and in forms such as diamond, graphite, and charcoal.
A salt or ester of nitric acid, containing the nitrate ion NO₃⁻.
A chemical compound in which oxygen is combined with another element or group of elements.
A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed or permanently changed.
A poisonous substance injected by some animals, such as snakes, spiders, and scorpions, through a bite or sting.
A substance formed when two or more chemical elements combine in fixed proportions.
A tough, fibrous protein that forms the main structural component of connective tissues such as skin, bones, cartilage, tendons, and ligaments.
A substance used to produce thrust or pressure, especially to propel a rocket, projectile, or other object.
One of two or more atoms of the same chemical element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, and therefore different atomic masses.
A stable subatomic particle with a positive electric charge, found in the nucleus of an atom; the number of protons determines the atom's atomic number.
A salt or ester of sulfuric acid, containing the sulfate ion SO₄²⁻.
A chemical compound containing one or more hydroxyl groups, especially a compound formed when a metal or positive ion combines with the hydroxide ion (OH⁻).
A salt or ester of phosphoric acid, containing phosphorus and oxygen, often used in fertilizers, detergents, and biological processes.
A positively charged polyatomic ion, NH₄⁺, formed when ammonia accepts a proton; it occurs in many salts and behaves chemically somewhat like an alkali-metal ion.
A pale-blue gas with a sharp smell, consisting of three oxygen atoms per molecule and formed naturally in the atmosphere or used as a disinfectant.
A chemical compound containing two oxygen atoms combined with one atom of another element.
A chemical compound containing fluorine, especially a salt of hydrofluoric acid; commonly added to toothpaste or drinking water to help prevent tooth decay.
A chemical compound in which sulfur is combined with a less electronegative element, especially a compound containing the sulfide ion S²⁻.
A chemical compound whose molecules contain one oxygen atom bonded to another element.
A hard mineral compound consisting of silicon and oxygen, commonly found in sand, quartz, and many rocks; silicon dioxide.
A salt or ester containing silicon, oxygen, and usually one or more metals, based on the silicate anion or its structural units; silicates make up many common minerals and rocks.
A colorless, flammable hydrocarbon gas with the chemical formula C₂H₄, used industrially to make plastics and other chemicals and naturally produced by plants to regulate fruit ripening.
A colorless, volatile, flammable, poisonous alcohol used as a solvent, fuel, and industrial chemical.
A simple sugar found naturally in fruits, honey, and some vegetables; it has the same chemical formula as glucose but a different molecular structure.
A colorless, highly flammable liquid aromatic hydrocarbon with the chemical formula C₆H₆, used as an industrial solvent and in manufacturing; it is toxic and carcinogenic.
A colorless, strong-smelling, highly reactive gas used in manufacturing resins, plastics, textiles, and disinfectants, and commonly encountered in dilute aqueous solution.
A highly poisonous chemical compound containing the cyanide ion (CN−), commonly referring to hydrogen cyanide or a cyanide salt.
An ion with a negative electrical charge, formed when an atom or molecule gains one or more electrons.

A male sex hormone produced mainly in the testes, and in smaller amounts by the ovaries and adrenal glands, that supports the development of male reproductive tissues and secondary sex characteristics.
A colorless, highly flammable gaseous hydrocarbon (C₃H₈), commonly stored as a liquid under pressure and used as a fuel for heating, cooking, and vehicles.
A green pigment in plants, algae, and some bacteria that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
A chemical compound containing an oxygen–oxygen bond, especially one used as an oxidizing agent or disinfectant.
A salt containing the bicarbonate ion (HCO₃⁻), especially sodium bicarbonate, commonly known as baking soda.

A nitrogen-containing chemical compound, CO(NH₂)₂, produced in the liver from the breakdown of proteins and excreted in urine; it is also manufactured for use in fertilizers, plastics, and other products.
A chemical reaction in which a compound is broken down by reacting with water, often producing new substances from the compound’s components.
A colorless, highly flammable liquid ketone used as a solvent, especially in products such as nail-polish remover, and as an industrial chemical.
The dried leaves, flowers, and stems of the cannabis plant, used as a psychoactive drug.
A very light, colorless, odorless, chemically inert noble gas with the atomic number 2, used in balloons, cooling systems, and scientific applications.
A hard, lightweight, silver-gray chemical element with the symbol Be and atomic number 4.
A chemical element with the symbol B and atomic number 5, occurring as a hard, brittle metalloid and used in materials, glass, detergents, and some agricultural products.
A highly reactive, pale-yellow chemical element with the atomic number 9; a halogen that exists as a poisonous diatomic gas under ordinary conditions.
A colorless, odorless chemical element with the symbol Ne and atomic number 10, a noble gas used especially in lighting.
A light, silvery-white metallic chemical element with the symbol Mg and atomic number 12, used in alloys, flares, fireworks, and biological processes.
A hard, brittle chemical element with the symbol Si and atomic number 14, widely used in glassmaking, ceramics, and electronic components.
A highly reactive chemical element with the symbol P and atomic number 15, occurring in several forms, including white and red phosphorus.
A yellow, nonmetallic chemical element with the symbol S and atomic number 16.
A colorless, odorless, chemically inert noble gas with the atomic number 18, used especially in light bulbs, welding, and protective atmospheres.
A soft, highly reactive chemical element with the symbol K and atomic number 19, an essential mineral and electrolyte in living organisms.
A soft, silvery-white chemical element with the symbol Ca and atomic number 20, important in the formation of bones and teeth and present in many minerals and foods.
A soft, silvery-white metallic chemical element with the atomic number 21 and the symbol Sc.
A strong, lightweight, corrosion-resistant chemical element with the symbol Ti and atomic number 22, used in alloys, aircraft, medical implants, and other products.
A hard, silvery-gray metallic chemical element with the symbol V and atomic number 23, used chiefly to strengthen steel and in some chemical compounds.
A hard, shiny, steel-gray chemical element with the symbol Cr and atomic number 24, used in alloys, stainless steel, and protective or decorative coatings.
A hard, brittle, silvery-gray chemical element with atomic number 25, used mainly in steelmaking, batteries, and other industrial applications.
A hard, silvery-blue chemical element with the symbol Co and atomic number 27, used in alloys, batteries, pigments, and other industrial applications.
A chemical element with the symbol Ni and atomic number 28, used in alloys and plating.
A soft, silvery chemical element with the symbol Ga and atomic number 31, which melts slightly above room temperature.
A rare, hard, brittle, gray-white chemical element with the symbol Ge and atomic number 32, used chiefly as a semiconductor and in infrared optics.
A toxic chemical element with the symbol As and atomic number 33, occurring naturally in minerals and used in some industrial processes.
A nonmetallic chemical element with the symbol Se and atomic number 34, used in electronics, glassmaking, pigments, and some industrial processes.
A toxic, reddish-brown, volatile chemical element with atomic number 35 and symbol Br; at room temperature it is a liquid and belongs to the halogen group.
A colorless, odorless, chemically inert noble gas with the atomic number 36, found in trace amounts in the atmosphere and used in lighting and some specialized technologies.
A soft, silvery-white chemical element with the symbol Rb and atomic number 37.
A soft, silvery-white chemical element with the symbol Sr and atomic number 38, occurring naturally in minerals and used in some pyrotechnics, ceramics, and medical applications.
A soft, silvery metallic chemical element with the symbol Y and atomic number 39, used chiefly in alloys, phosphors, lasers, and certain electronic components.
A hard, gray-white metallic chemical element with the symbol Zr and atomic number 40, valued for its resistance to corrosion and used in nuclear reactors, ceramics, and chemical equipment.
A chemical element with the symbol Nb and atomic number 41, a soft, gray, corrosion-resistant transition metal used in alloys, superconducting materials, and specialized industrial applications.
A hard, silvery-gray chemical element with the symbol Mo and atomic number 42, used mainly to strengthen steel and other alloys.
A chemical element with the symbol Tc and atomic number 43; a silvery-gray, radioactive metal produced artificially and used in some medical imaging procedures.
A rare, hard, silvery-white chemical element with the atomic number 44, belonging to the platinum group of metals.
A rare, hard, silvery-white chemical element with the symbol Rh and atomic number 45, used especially in catalytic converters and to plate jewelry.
A rare, silvery-white chemical element with the symbol Pd and atomic number 46, used especially in catalytic converters, electronics, and jewelry.
A soft, silvery-white chemical element with the symbol Cd and atomic number 48, used especially in batteries, pigments, coatings, and alloys.
A soft, silvery-white chemical element with the symbol In and atomic number 49, used chiefly in semiconductors, alloys, and transparent conductive coatings.
A brittle, silvery-white chemical element with the symbol Sb and atomic number 51, used in alloys, flame retardants, semiconductors, and other industrial applications.
A rare, brittle, silvery-white chemical element with the symbol Te and atomic number 52.
A chemical element with the symbol I and atomic number 53, a lustrous dark blue-black solid that readily forms a violet vapor and is essential in small amounts for thyroid function.
A heavy, colorless, chemically inert noble gas with the atomic number 54, used in lighting, lasers, and some medical applications.
A soft, silvery-gold chemical element with the atomic number 55 and the symbol Cs; it is an extremely reactive alkali metal.
A soft, silvery-white chemical element with the symbol Ba and atomic number 56.
A soft, silvery-white chemical element with the atomic number 57; a reactive rare-earth metal.
A soft, silvery metallic chemical element with the atomic number 58, belonging to the lanthanide series.
A soft, silvery metallic chemical element with the atomic number 59, belonging to the lanthanide series; its symbol is Pr.
A soft, silvery-white chemical element with the symbol Nd and atomic number 60, used especially in strong permanent magnets, lasers, and specialized glass.

A radioactive chemical element with the symbol Pm and atomic number 61, belonging to the lanthanide series; it has no stable isotopes and is used mainly in specialized scientific and industrial applications.
A soft, silvery-white metallic chemical element with the symbol Sm and atomic number 62, used chiefly in magnets, lasers, and specialized industrial applications.
A soft, silvery-white chemical element with the symbol Eu and atomic number 63, one of the rare-earth metals.
A soft, silvery-white chemical element with the atomic number 64, belonging to the lanthanide series; its symbol is Gd.
A soft, silvery-white chemical element with the symbol Tb and atomic number 65, belonging to the lanthanide series.
A chemical element with the symbol Dy and atomic number 66, a soft, silvery rare-earth metal used in specialized magnets, lasers, and other technologies.
A chemical element with the symbol Ho and atomic number 67; a soft, silvery-white rare-earth metal.
A soft, silvery-white chemical element with the atomic number 68, used in lasers, optical fibers, and specialized alloys.
A soft, silvery metallic chemical element with the symbol Tm and atomic number 69, belonging to the lanthanide series.
A soft, silvery metallic chemical element with the symbol Yb and atomic number 70, belonging to the lanthanide series.
A chemical element with the atomic number 71, a silvery-white metal in the lanthanide series.
A chemical element with the symbol Hf and atomic number 72, a silvery-gray metal used chiefly in nuclear reactors and high-temperature alloys.
A rare, hard, corrosion-resistant chemical element with the atomic number 73, used especially in electronic capacitors and specialized alloys.

A hard, dense, grayish-white chemical element with the symbol W and atomic number 74, known for its extremely high melting point and used in alloys, electrical contacts, and high-temperature applications.
A rare, silvery-white metallic chemical element with the atomic number 75, used especially in high-temperature alloys and catalysts.
A hard, bluish-white chemical element, the densest naturally occurring element, with the symbol Os and atomic number 76.
A hard, brittle, silvery-white chemical element with the symbol Ir and atomic number 77, belonging to the platinum group of metals.
A dense, valuable, silvery-white metallic chemical element, used especially in jewelry, laboratory equipment, and industrial catalysts.
A heavy, silvery metallic chemical element that is liquid at ordinary room temperature and is used in thermometers, electrical devices, and some industrial processes.
A soft, malleable, bluish-white chemical element with the symbol Tl and atomic number 81.
A brittle, silvery-white chemical element with the symbol Bi and atomic number 83.
A rare, highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Po and atomic number 84.
A rare, highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol At and atomic number 85, belonging to the halogen group.
A colorless, odorless, radioactive noble gas produced naturally by the decay of uranium and radium, capable of accumulating indoors and posing a health risk.
A highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Fr and atomic number 87, belonging to the alkali metals.
A highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Ra and atomic number 88, occurring naturally in uranium ores.
A radioactive metallic chemical element with the symbol Ac and atomic number 89, occurring naturally in trace amounts and used mainly as a source of alpha radiation and in scientific research.
A naturally occurring radioactive chemical element with the symbol Th and atomic number 90, a silvery metal used in nuclear technology and some specialized applications.
A radioactive chemical element with the symbol Pa and atomic number 91, occurring naturally in uranium ores and used mainly for scientific research.
A heavy, radioactive chemical element with the symbol U and atomic number 92, occurring naturally in several isotopes and used as a source of nuclear energy and in weapons.
A radioactive chemical element with the symbol Np and atomic number 93, a silvery metal produced mainly in nuclear reactions.
A radioactive chemical element with the atomic number 94, represented by the symbol Pu, used mainly in nuclear weapons and some nuclear reactors.
A synthetic radioactive chemical element with the symbol Am and atomic number 95, belonging to the actinide series.
A radioactive chemical element with the symbol Cm and atomic number 96, a synthetic actinide metal named after Marie and Pierre Curie.
A synthetic radioactive chemical element with the symbol Bk and atomic number 97, belonging to the actinide series.
A highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Cf and atomic number 98, produced synthetically and used mainly as a neutron source.
A highly radioactive synthetic chemical element with the atomic number 99, classified as an actinide and represented by the symbol Es.
A synthetic radioactive chemical element with the symbol Fm and atomic number 100, produced in nuclear reactions and named after physicist Enrico Fermi.
A synthetic, radioactive chemical element with the symbol Md and atomic number 101, produced in tiny amounts in laboratories.
A synthetic radioactive chemical element with the symbol No and atomic number  Nobelium 102, produced artificially and named after Alfred Nobel.
A radioactive, synthetic chemical element with the symbol Lr and atomic number 103, belonging to the actinide series.
A synthetic radioactive chemical element with atomic number 104, symbol Rf, and belonging to the transactinide metals.
A synthetic, radioactive chemical element with the symbol Db and atomic number 105.
A highly radioactive synthetic chemical element with atomic number 106 and symbol Sg, produced in laboratories and named after chemist Glenn T. Seaborg.
A synthetic, highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Bh and atomic number 107.
A synthetic, highly radioactive chemical element with the atomic number 108 and the symbol Hs.
A synthetic radioactive chemical element with the atomic number 109 and the symbol Mt; a highly unstable transactinide metal produced only in laboratories.
A synthetic, highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol Ds and atomic number 110.
A highly radioactive synthetic chemical element with the atomic number 111 and the symbol Rg.
A synthetic, highly radioactive chemical element with the atomic number 112 and symbol Cn.
A synthetic chemical element with the atomic number 113 and the symbol Nh; a highly radioactive transactinide metal.
A synthetic, highly radioactive chemical element with the atomic number 114 and symbol Fl.
A synthetic chemical element with atomic number 115, symbol Mc, and an extremely unstable radioactive isotope; it is a transactinide element named after the Moscow region.
A highly radioactive synthetic chemical element with the symbol Lv and atomic number 116.
A synthetic chemical element with atomic number 117, a highly radioactive halogen produced artificially; its symbol is Ts.
A synthetic, highly radioactive chemical element with the atomic number 118, symbol Og, and the heaviest currently named element.
